content.title: About
content.content: Chinese broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra), also known as gai lan, is a cruciferous vegetable. Raw Chinese broccoli has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. It is commonly used in salads, pickles, and as an ingredient in Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chinese broccoli differs from regular green broccoli by its lighter, almost white head and more tender florets.
In China it is called “gai lan” and has been cultivated for over 2,000 years.
It is rich in glucosinolates, which break down into compounds with anti‑cancer properties.
Raw Chinese broccoli retains more vitamins than when it is cooked.
Unlike standard broccoli, Chinese varieties are often grown in warmer climates.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Raw Chinese broccoli provides over 100 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: For some people raw broccoli can cause gas and bloating due to its raffinose content.

items.title: Possible allergies
items.content: Allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables are rare but possible.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: High vitamin K levels may affect the efficacy of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw Chinese broccoli can be thinly sliced and added to salads, used in spring rolls, pickled, or served with a dipping sauce made from soy sauce and sesame oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store broccoli in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a small amount of moisture. Use within 3–5 days. Discard if yellow spots or off‑odors develop.

content.title: About
content.content: Cake, cupcake and gingerbread are baked goods made from flour, sugar, eggs and fats, often flavored with spices, fruit or chocolate. Cake is usually layered and frosted, cupcake is denser and single‑serve, while gingerbread is a traditional spiced cookie popular in colder seasons.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cakes have cultural variations: in Russia a "honey cake" is served at weddings, in Japan a "sofu cake" is a specialty.
Cupcakes earned the nickname "American" due to their surge in popularity in the United States in the early 20th century.
Gingerbread originated in medieval Europe as a medicinal confection made with ginger and honey.
In the United States, over 200 million gingerbread cookies are sold each Christmas season.
Traditional German "Lebkuchen" is considered the ancestor of modern gingerbread.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrate content in cake, cupcake and gingerbread provides a quick source of energy.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Spices such as ginger, cinnamon and clove contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger in gingerbread stimulates gastric secretions and can aid digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour in cakes and cupcakes supply vitamins B1, B2 and B6.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Flour and nuts, often added to recipes, provide magnesium, iron and zinc.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large portions may raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Cakes and cupcakes frequently contain nuts, dairy and eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Using margarine or partially hydrogenated oils can introduce trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cake in slices, often with fruit or berry sauce. Cupcakes are convenient as a snack, halved if desired. Gingerbread is commonly enjoyed with tea, glazed or dusted with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep baked goods in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 1 week) or freeze (up to 3 months). Gingerbread stays best in a dry place to stay crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Catfish fillet is the flesh of a freshwater catfish, prepared by deep‑frying. The fish has a firm, white meat with a mild flavor that becomes richer when fried. It is commonly served as steaks, strips, or bite‑size pieces coated in breadcrumbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Catfish can grow over a meter long, but culinary uses usually involve younger, smaller specimens.
In many countries (e.g., the United States, Russia, and China) catfish is a popular fast‑food item and is often featured in fish‑and‑chips style dishes.
High‑heat frying creates a crispy crust while preserving most of the protein and essential amino acids.
Compared with many other fried fish products, catfish has relatively low fat content when lightly breaded.
Traditional Southeast Asian cuisines often marinate catfish in spices before frying.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Catfish provides about 18–20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and helps maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Unlike many marine fish, catfish typically contains low levels of mercury, making it safer for frequent consumption.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3 fatty acids in catfish can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to catfish.

items.title: Calorie‑dense
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories and fat, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Catfish raised in polluted waters may contain heavy metals; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Trans fats from reused oil
items.content: Reusing frying oil can create trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Catfish fillets are typically deep‑fried in vegetable oil until golden brown. Serve with lemon wedges, tartar sauce, fresh salads, or in a sandwich. For a lighter option, bake in the oven with a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried catfish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-m.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with a creamy sauce and meat pieces is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. It combines whole‑grain pasta, a smooth cream sauce, and selected meat, providing a balanced mix of carbohydrates, protein, and fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta retains more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
The cream sauce is typically made from dairy and often fortified with B‑vitamins.
The meat is usually chicken or turkey, making the dish leaner than beef‑based versions.
Ready‑to‑heat meals often contain small amounts of preservatives to extend shelf life.
Microwave heating preserves most nutrients when the recommended time is followed.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The meat component supplies complete protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce is often enriched with calcium and vitamin D, which are important for bone health.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Modern formulations aim to eliminate trans fats, making the product heart‑friendlier.

items.title: Convenient and quick
items.content: A ready‑to‑heat meal saves time while delivering a nutritious lunch or dinner.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared meals can be high in salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream sauce may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some packages use preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave cold spots where bacteria might survive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in the microwave for 2–3 minutes, then stir to distribute the sauce evenly. Optionally top with fresh herbs or grated cheese for extra flavor. The dish can also be served alongside a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place at 10 °C–25 °C. Once opened, keep the product refrigerated and consume within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw hot peppers are the fruits of Capsicum plants that are eaten fresh. They have a pronounced spiciness, distinctive aroma, and a crisp texture. Peppers are commonly used in salads, sauces, marinades, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The heat of peppers is measured on the Scoville scale; the hottest known variety is the Carolina Reaper, exceeding 1.5 million SHU.
Capsaicin is the main active compound responsible for the burning sensation and also has analgesic properties.
Peppers are botanically related to tomatoes, eggplants, and potatoes.
Raw peppers are rich in vitamin C: a single medium pepper provides more than 100 % of the daily requirement.
In some cultures, peppers are used in traditional medicine to aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, supports collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin may increase metabolism, aid fat burning, and has anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and skin health.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A medium pepper contains about 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Mucous membrane irritation
items.content: Capsaicin can cause burning in the mouth, stomach, and intestines, especially when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergy to peppers, resulting in skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Capsaicin may enhance the effects of anticoagulants, so people on such medication should use caution.

items.title: Skin irritation
items.content: When handling hot peppers, wearing gloves is advisable to prevent skin burns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw hot peppers can be sliced and added to salads, salsas, marinades, or used as a spicy garnish. They may also be lightly sautéed to mellow the heat while retaining freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peppers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely wrapped in a perforated bag. They stay fresh for 1‑2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze sliced pieces in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato chips, popped, NFS are light, crunchy snacks made by puffing thinly sliced potatoes without added oil. They have a delicate texture, a classic potato flavor, and lower fat content compared with traditional fried chips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puffing works by rapid moisture evaporation, creating a porous structure without the need for oil frying.
The NFS (National Food Service) brand is known for products aimed at corporate catering and bulk foodservice.
Popped chips are often featured in diet menus because they contain fewer calories than regular fried chips.
A wide range of flavors is available: classic salted, cheese, barbecue, and spicy chili.
The puffing process helps retain more vitamin C, which is usually lost during deep‑frying.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Because no oil is used during production, popped chips contain significantly less fat, making them a better choice for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide starch that supplies steady energy and helps maintain blood‑sugar levels when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Puffed potatoes retain some vitamin C, an antioxidant that supports the immune system.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal muscle and nerve function and helps regulate fluid balance.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: The product contains no gluten, making it safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some flavored varieties are high in salt, which may be a concern for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens in seasonings
items.content: Flavor additives can contain dairy or soy ingredients that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Possible preservatives
items.content: To extend shelf life, anti‑oxidants may be used, which are not suitable for all consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popped chips are convenient as a standalone snack, tossed into salads for crunch, served with dips, or used in recipes as a lighter alternative to traditional fried chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.
